# Introduction {#sec:intro}

Factor returns enter empirical asset pricing tests, optimal portfolio allocation, and risk-management decisions. Constructing them typically involves a three-stage pipeline: data acquisition, usually downloading and cleaning raw return and accounting data from the Center for Research in Security Prices (CRSP) and Compustat; variable construction, including appropriate lags to avoid look-ahead bias; and portfolio sorting, where securities are assigned to portfolios based on characteristics. Each stage involves consequential design choices such as how to handle delistings, which fiscal-year lag to apply, where to set breakpoints, and whether portfolios should be equal- or value-weighted. Few pipelines are standardized, and fewer still ship with executable code. Therefore, reproducing or extending a factor series often starts with reconstructing the pipeline from scratch, with no way to verify that the result matches the original approach.

No widely adopted tool covers this upstream workflow end to end. Ken French's Data Library [@fama.2023], the most popular factor source, publishes returns without the code that produced them. Projects that do publish code [@chen.2022; @jensen.2023; @dickerson.2023] release fixed scripts rather than configurable functions, and PyBondLab [@rossetti.2026] exposes portfolio sorts for corporate bonds but leaves data acquisition and cleaning to the user. Yet construction choices matter: @walter.2024 and @soebhag.2024 show that they materially change the outcome of portfolio sorts. Existing \proglang{R} packages for quantitative finance work downstream, on price and return panels that the user must already have. Between raw data and standard asset-pricing tests sits an opaque layer in which construction choices accumulate silently.

This paper introduces \CRANpkg{tidyfinance}, an \proglang{R} package on CRAN that exposes each stage of the pipeline as configurable code. The package addresses each stage with a dedicated interface. A unified `download_data()` function cleans, aligns, and harmonizes panels from Wharton Research Data Services (WRDS), Ken French's Data Library, Federal Reserve Economic Data (FRED), and `r length(setdiff(unique(tidyfinance::list_supported_datasets()$domain), c("WRDS", "Fama-French", "FRED", "Pseudo Data")))` other providers. The WRDS panels cover CRSP, Compustat, the Trade Reporting and Compliance Engine (TRACE), and the Mergent Fixed Income Securities Database (FISD). Composable helpers then automate fiscal-year lagging, breakpoint computation, and portfolio aggregation. Every construction choice is exposed as a function argument with a default that follows established convention (for instance, value-weights and the Fama-French fiscal-year lag). A default call reproduces standard practice; overriding any default takes one argument.

We illustrate the package by reproducing a version of the asset growth factor of @cooper.2008 end-to-end from raw CRSP and Compustat data, then varying any construction choice with a single-argument change. The package operationalizes the workflow developed in the open-access textbook *Tidy Finance with \proglang{R}* [@scheuch.2023], which presents each step in tutorial form with inline scripts. The contribution of this paper is \CRANpkg{tidyfinance} itself: a unified, configurable, tested, and versioned \proglang{R} package for this workflow. Where the book teaches a reader how to assemble the pipeline from scratch, the package supplies it as a single package that researchers can install, call, audit, and reuse without rebuilding the underlying code.

# Background and related work {#sec:background}

The \proglang{R} ecosystem for empirical asset pricing splits into three groups. Each addresses a particular part of the workflow and leaves the rest to the user.

**Data-acquisition packages.** Several \proglang{R} packages retrieve data sources common in asset pricing, but none covers the WRDS-CRSP-Compustat panel or the cleaning, alignment, and survivorship conventions the literature requires. \CRANpkg{frenchdata} [@frenchdata.2021] downloads and parses the archives of Ken French's Data Library. \CRANpkg{quantmod} [@ryan.2025] and \CRANpkg{tidyquant} [@dancho.2026] cover price series from Yahoo Finance, FRED, and Tiingo, and \CRANpkg{Rblpapi} [@armstrong.Rblpapi] queries the Bloomberg terminal. None of them implements a factor-construction step.

**Downstream analysis packages.** Once a cleaned panel is in hand, several packages support analysis. \CRANpkg{PerformanceAnalytics} [@peterson.2026] computes performance and risk metrics for return series. \CRANpkg{fPortfolio} [@wuertz.fPortfolio] covers portfolio optimization. \CRANpkg{RQuantLib} [@eddelbuettel.RQuantLib] interfaces with QuantLib for derivative pricing. \CRANpkg{highfrequency} [@boudt.highfrequency] cleans intraday trade-and-quote panels and implements microstructure-volatility estimators. Each of these tools assumes that the panel of returns and factors is already constructed; none implements a factor-construction layer.

**Factor data releases.** A group of projects publishes *factor return series* directly. Ken French's Data Library [@fama.2023] supplies the canonical @fama.1993 three- and five-factor returns and dozens of sorted portfolios, but documents construction in prose only and provides no associated code. @akey.2026 show that these series change retroactively as the underlying method is revised, so that the factor returns a researcher obtains depend on *when* they were downloaded, with material effects on mutual-fund performance and cross-sectional asset pricing tests. Three more recent projects pair the published factor data with the construction script that produced it. @hou.2020 replicate 452 anomalies and find that most fail to clear conventional significance once microcaps are down-weighted with NYSE breakpoints and value-weighted returns. The Open Source Cross-Sectional Asset Pricing repository [@chen.2022] responds by publishing per-anomaly construction scripts alongside the resulting 212 long-short returns. The Open Source Bond Asset Pricing project [@dickerson.2023] does the same for corporate bond factors. @jensen.2023 provide the Global Factor Data of 153 long-short factors across 93 countries, together with the construction code in \proglang{Python}. These projects let a reader inspect how each factor was built and reproduce its returns, but two limitations remain. First, none of these releases exposes its pipeline as a callable API. A user who wants the asset growth factor rebalanced in January instead of July, or formed on NYSE-plus-NASDAQ breakpoints, or computed on a different fiscal-year lag, must fork the published script and edit it by hand. Second, the factor returns are frozen at the release date, with no in-workflow path to refresh them as new observations arrive or as a researcher's design choices evolve.

**\CRANpkg{tidyfinance} fills the missing gap:** the package supplies the cleaned WRDS-CRSP-Compustat panel that data-acquisition packages do not produce and exposes the factor-construction pipeline that downstream analysis packages assume to be in hand. One `download_data()` call returns a cleaned WRDS-CRSP-Compustat panel; further functions implement the full factor-construction pipeline (fiscal-year lagging, breakpoint computation, portfolio sorting, long-short aggregation) as a chain of composable steps whose arguments cover the construction choices that vary across studies in the literature above. Two design principles, both inherited from @scheuch.2023, guide the API. First, each construction decision is *transparent*: it appears as a configurable parameter with a documented default, in line with the tidy tools principles of @wickham.2023. Second, the pipeline is *modular* by construction: each construction step is implemented as a narrowly scoped function with clearly defined inputs and outputs. Researchers can therefore either chain these functions into a complete factor-construction workflow or reuse individual components within their own pipelines.

**Factor-construction software outside \proglang{R}.** PyBondLab [@rossetti.2026], a \proglang{Python} package on PyPI since July 2024 and developed alongside the Open Source Bond Asset Pricing project, implements portfolio sorts for corporate bonds as a callable API. Like \CRANpkg{tidyfinance}, it offers single and double sorts with staggered rebalancing over overlapping holding periods. Beyond \CRANpkg{tidyfinance}, it sorts bonds within each issuer, forms factors on many signals in a single call, and reports portfolio turnover. Its banding option lowers that turnover by keeping a bond in its previous portfolio unless its new portfolio rank differs by a set number of portfolios. \CRANpkg{tidyfinance} differs in three respects. First, it integrates data acquisition and cleaning, so that the pipeline starts from raw WRDS panels rather than a user-supplied panel. Second, it targets equities and exposes equity-specific construction choices such as capped value weights and industry and earnings screens. Third, it pairs portfolio sorts with Fama-MacBeth regressions. The two packages thus complement each other across asset classes and languages.

# Package overview {#sec:overview}

## Installation and setup {#sec:installation}

You can install the released version of \CRANpkg{tidyfinance} [from CRAN](https://cran.r-project.org/package=tidyfinance) via:

```{r install-tidyfinance-cran, eval=FALSE, purl=FALSE}
install.packages("tidyfinance")
```

To install the development version of \CRANpkg{tidyfinance} from [GitHub](https://github.com/tidy-finance/r-tidyfinance), first install \CRANpkg{remotes}, then run:

```{r install-tidyfinance-dev, eval=FALSE, purl=FALSE}
install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("tidy-finance/r-tidyfinance")
```

Once installed, load the package with: 
```{r load-tidyfinance-initial}
library("tidyfinance")
```

## Design and workflow {#sec:design}

The empirical asset pricing workflow decomposes into three stages: data acquisition, variable construction, and portfolio sorting. Each stage involves dozens of small decisions: sample filters, cleaning rules, rebalancing conventions, and breakpoint definitions. Table \@ref(tab:functions) catalogs the user-facing functions exported by \CRANpkg{tidyfinance}, grouped by workflow stage. The remainder of this section walks through them in narrative order.

\setlength{\tabcolsep}{4pt}
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.0}
```

| Function                                 | Purpose                                                             |
+==========================================+=====================================================================+
| *Data acquisition*                       |                                                                     |
+------------------------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------------+
| `download_data()`                        | Retrieves and cleans a panel from supported data providers.         |
+------------------------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------------+
| `set_wrds_credentials()`                 | Stores WRDS username and password in `.Renviron` for subsequent     |
|                                          | calls.                                                              |
+------------------------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------------+
| \rule{0pt}{3ex}*Variable construction*   |                                                                     |
+------------------------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------------+

+------------------------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------------+

|                                          | the same windowing logic.                                           |
+------------------------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------------+

|                                          | the corresponding quantile.                                         |
+------------------------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------------+

A first illustration uses only public data. A single call downloads and parses the Fama-French three-factor data from Ken French's Data Library:

```{r example-ff-factors}
ff_factors <- download_data(
  domain = "Fama-French",
  dataset = "Fama/French 3 Factors",
  start_date = "1972-01-01",
  end_date = "2024-12-31"
)
```

The `start_date` and `end_date` arguments generalize across every dataset type in Table \@ref(tab:data-sources) that supports a time dimension.

Public data still requires nontrivial cleaning. Ken French's files, for instance, code missing values as $-99.99$ or $-999$, report returns in percent, use column labels such as `Mkt-RF`, and store dates as `YYYYMM` integers. `download_data()` turns the codes into `NA`, rescales returns to decimals, renames the columns (e.g., `mkt_excess`), and returns a proper `date` column. Similarly, with `domain = "Goyal-Welch"`, `download_data()` parses the raw spreadsheet of the @goyal.2008 predictors at monthly, quarterly, or annual frequency (set via `dataset`) and constructs the standard equity-premium predictors, such as the log dividend-price ratio (`dp`), the term spread (`tms`), and the default-yield spread (`dfy`).

For empirical asset pricing work, WRDS is the common source of return and accounting panels. WRDS data are proprietary and require an institutional subscription and credentials. \CRANpkg{tidyfinance} handles this setup once. `set_wrds_credentials()` prompts for the username and password and stores them in a project-specific or global `.Renviron` file, and prompts the user to add `.Renviron` to `.gitignore` to prevent credential leakage. Subsequent `download_data()` calls open the database connection automatically. Credentials alone do not suffice: before the first connection, users must enroll in WRDS two-factor authentication (2FA) and accept the WRDS terms of use on the WRDS website. With push notifications enabled, each connection then triggers a 2FA push to the registered device; once approved, the connection proceeds normally. Without push, a successful 2FA login on the WRDS website from the same IP address authorizes connections from that address for 30 days. The help page `?get_wrds_connection` lists the full setup checklist.

`download_data()` applies standard cleaning conventions following @bali.2016 and @scheuch.2023 automatically. For CRSP monthly data, the function restricts the universe to common equity securities listed on NYSE, AMEX (now NYSE American), or NASDAQ. It computes market capitalization as shares outstanding times price, constructs a one-month market capitalization lag for portfolio weights, and maps listing exchange codes and Standard Industrial Classification (SIC) codes to readable labels. Excess returns are raw returns minus a risk-free rate that \CRANpkg{tidyfinance} constructs from FRED by splicing the 3-month Treasury bill secondary-market rate (pre-2001) with the 4-week Treasury bill secondary-market rate (from 2001 onward). The spliced series is hosted on Hugging Face and refreshed monthly by a scheduled GitHub Actions workflow. The function drops observations with missing returns or market capitalization, and incorporates delisting returns directly, eliminating the need for a separate adjustment. The function defaults to the CRSP 2.0 (CIZ) layout first introduced in July 2022. Alternatively, passing `version = "v1"` returns the legacy (SIZ) layout, which ends in December 2024. @schwarz.2026 document that the move to CIZ rewrites a non-trivial share of historical monthly returns through a changed dividend reinvestment assumption, yet find that average premia and their significance are largely unaffected.

For Compustat annual data, `download_data()` restricts to industrial-format consolidated statements and retains only the most recent observation per firm-year. Following @fama.1992, it constructs book equity in priority order: stockholders' equity when available, else common equity plus preferred stock, else total assets minus total liabilities. The function adds back deferred taxes and investment tax credits, and subtracts the book value of preferred stock.

For TRACE corporate bond transactions, `download_data()` applies the Dick-Nielsen cleaning protocol [@dicknielsen.2009] to remove cancellations, corrections, and reversals before returning the trade panel.

Across `download_data()`, every returned panel exposes a single `date` column of `<date>` type, regardless of source. Joining observations from different providers therefore reduces to an equality join on `date` without manual format conversion. The convention is the same across frequencies: daily observations return the trading date, monthly observations the first calendar day of the reference month (regardless of whether it was a trading day), and quarterly and annual observations the first day of the fiscal period-end month as reported by the original source. For Compustat, the latter is the firm's fiscal period-end (`datadate`). Macroeconomic series from FRED keep their original release dates. Where the underlying source uses an internal date that differs from this convention, \CRANpkg{tidyfinance} preserves it as an auxiliary column: CRSP 2.0 monthly returns, for example, retain the trading-date `mthcaldt` as `calculation_date` alongside the harmonized `date`.

## Variable construction {#sec:variable-construction}

Most predictive variables in asset pricing studies use lagged information so that, for example, portfolio formation in month $t$ uses only data observable at the end of month $t-1$. `add_lagged_columns()` automates the required lagging procedure. For each row in the data, it looks back over a configurable window and attaches the most recent observed value of the chosen columns. By default (`ff_adjustment = FALSE`), the window is bounded by `lag` (the minimum delay between observation and use) and `max_lag` (the maximum delay before a stale value is treated as missing). Within this window, the function picks the most recent value, skipping missing values if `drop_na = TRUE`, as needed for monthly panels whose accounting columns are only filled at fiscal year-ends; if no observation falls in the window, the lagged column takes `NA`.

The second mode, enabled by `ff_adjustment = TRUE`, implements the Fama-French convention [@fama.1993]. The convention assumes accounting variables for fiscal year $t-1$ become public information by June of year $t$, then uses them for portfolio formation from July of $t$ through June of $t+1$. This timing produces a step-function lag that updates once per year at the June/July boundary, regardless of the underlying fiscal year-end, and ignores `lag` and `max_lag`. The two modes differ: with a 7-month lag, a firm with a June year-end updates in January, but under the convention it updates in July, like a firm with a December year-end. If a fiscal year is missing, the lag window drops the old value 18 months after its fiscal year-end, while the convention drops it at the next July.

`join_lagged_values()` applies the same logic, including `ff_adjustment`, when it merges lagged values from one data frame into another with a different frequency, for example, annual accounting data into a monthly return panel.

A handful of additional helpers cover routine operations that recur across empirical studies. `winsorize()` and `trim()` handle outliers in cross-sectional variables: the former symmetrically replaces values below the $q$-th and above the $(1-q)$-th percentile with the corresponding quantile values, while the latter sets them to `NA`. `estimate_model()` fits a linear model from a formula string and returns the coefficients as a tidy data frame, which composes naturally with `group_by()` for grouped or rolling regressions such as estimating time-series factor exposures stock by stock via `estimate_betas()`. `compute_rolling_value()` applies an arbitrary aggregation function over a rolling window defined in calendar time rather than row counts, accommodating irregular observation frequencies and missing periods. `filter_sorting_data()` screens a panel before sorting, dropping observations that fail the sample filters bundled in a `filter_options()` object, such as financial or utility firms or stocks below a minimum price or size. By default, it reports how many observations each filter removes, which `quiet = TRUE` suppresses. 

## Portfolio sorting {#sec:portfolio-sorting}

A portfolio sort groups stocks each period into ordered portfolios according to the level of a sorting variable. The boundaries between portfolios are called *breakpoints*: numeric cutoffs of the sorting variable that determine which portfolio a stock joins. A quintile sort on size, for instance, has four breakpoints at the 20th, 40th, 60th, and 80th percentiles of the cross-sectional market-capitalization distribution. Common sorting variables include size (measured as market capitalization), beta, book-to-market, and momentum. The long-short return between the extreme portfolios is interpreted as a factor-mimicking strategy and serves as the basis for tests of whether the sorting variable forecasts future returns. Portfolio sorts are among the most widely used tools in empirical asset pricing [@bali.2016]. We expose the procedure through four composable building blocks plus a one-call wrapper.

`compute_breakpoints()` takes a cross-section and a sorting variable and returns the numeric cutoffs that define the portfolio boundaries. The user supplies either a number of portfolios (for example, five for quintiles) or an explicit vector of percentiles, but not both. A `breakpoints_exchanges` argument restricts the universe used to compute breakpoints. The standard convention is NYSE-listed stocks only, which prevents the large cross-section of small NASDAQ-listed firms from dominating the breakpoints [@fama.1993]. A related `breakpoints_min_size_threshold` argument excludes stocks below a market-cap quantile from the breakpoint computation, which size-related sorts often require because microcaps would otherwise distort the cutoffs. A `smooth_bunching` flag handles cases where the sorting variable takes the same value for many observations at the bottom or top of the distribution, so that the lowest (or highest) quantile breakpoints coincide. Without intervention, all tied observations would land in a single boundary portfolio while neighboring portfolios remain empty. When `smooth_bunching = TRUE`, the function assigns the bunched observations to the boundary portfolio and recomputes the remaining breakpoints on the subset of observations strictly inside the boundary value, restoring well-defined cutoffs for the interior portfolios.

`assign_portfolio()` maps each observation to a portfolio integer and uses breakpoints supplied either directly or via a breakpoint-computing function (defaulting to `compute_breakpoints()`). In practice, `assign_portfolio()` is called separately for each rebalancing date, so that portfolios are reformed each period rather than fixed once for the whole sample.

`compute_portfolio_returns()` ties the lower-level pieces together. Given a panel of stock data, one or two sorting variables, a sorting method, and `breakpoint_options`, it handles rebalancing, breakpoint computation, portfolio assignment, and return aggregation. It then returns a complete panel of portfolio returns. For each portfolio-date the function reports three return measures: equal-weighted, value-weighted using `mktcap_lag` as the weight, and capped value-weighted [@jensen.2023]. Following @jensen.2023, the capped version caps each stock's market capitalization at the `cap_weight` percentile of NYSE stocks on each date (default `0.8`, the 80th percentile), which prevents a few megacap firms from dominating the portfolio. A `min_portfolio_size` argument sets the minimum number of constituents below which the corresponding return is set to `NA`. An optional `rebalancing_month` argument switches from period-by-period rebalancing to annual rebalancing in the specified month. Portfolios formed in that month are then held constant for the following twelve months. Alternatively, `holding_period` and `skip` implement staggered rebalancing: portfolios are formed every period, and each cohort is held for `holding_period` periods, starting `skip` periods after formation, so that overlapping cohorts are averaged as in @jegadeesh.1993.

The function supports three sorting schemes, illustrated in Figure \@ref(fig:illustrate-portfolio-helper). A *univariate* sort uses a single variable. An *independent bivariate* sort computes breakpoints on each variable separately and intersects the resulting bins to produce a two-way grid. A *dependent bivariate* sort first partitions the cross-section by the secondary (control) variable and then re-sorts within each bucket on the main variable, which is the appropriate choice when the second variable is treated as a control rather than as an independent dimension of variation. For bivariate sorts, returns are averaged over the secondary variable so that only the main-variable portfolios are returned.

```{r simulate-portfolio-helper, echo=FALSE}
set.seed(3010)

n <- 1000
rho <- 0.6

f <- rnorm(n)

e1 <- rnorm(n)
e2 <- rnorm(n)

x1 <- f + sqrt(1 - rho^2) * e1
x2 <- f + sqrt(1 - rho^2) * e2

asset_growth <- pnorm(x1)
mktcap_lag <- pnorm(x2)

cross_section <- data.frame(asset_growth, mktcap_lag)
n_portfolio <- 2

breakpoints_ag <- cross_section |>
  compute_breakpoints(
    "asset_growth",
    breakpoint_options = breakpoint_options(n_portfolios = n_portfolio)
  )

portfolios_univariate <- cross_section |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    ag_portfolio = assign_portfolio(
      pick(everything()),
      "asset_growth",
      breakpoint_options = breakpoint_options(n_portfolios = n_portfolio)
    )
  )

portfolios_independent <- cross_section |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    ag_portfolio = assign_portfolio(
      pick(everything()),
      "asset_growth",
      breakpoint_options = breakpoint_options(n_portfolios = n_portfolio)
    ),
    size_portfolio = assign_portfolio(
      dplyr::pick(everything()),
      "mktcap_lag",
      breakpoint_options = breakpoint_options(n_portfolios = n_portfolio)
    ),
    portfolio_cell = paste0(ag_portfolio, "-", size_portfolio)
  )

portfolios_dependent <- cross_section |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    size_portfolio = assign_portfolio(
      dplyr::pick(everything()),
      "mktcap_lag",
      breakpoint_options = breakpoint_options(n_portfolios = n_portfolio)
    )
  ) |>
  dplyr::group_by(size_portfolio) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    ag_portfolio = assign_portfolio(
      dplyr::pick(everything()),
      "asset_growth",
      breakpoint_options = breakpoint_options(n_portfolios = n_portfolio)
    ),
    portfolio_cell = paste0(ag_portfolio, "-", size_portfolio)
  ) |>
  dplyr::ungroup()
```

```{r illustrate-portfolio-helper, fig.alt="Three scatterplots of a simulated cross-section showing univariate, independent bivariate, and dependent bivariate portfolio assignments, with asset-growth rank on the horizontal axis and size rank on the vertical axis.", echo=FALSE, fig.cap=paste0("Portfolio sort approaches illustrated on a simulated cross-section. Each panel plots simulated observations assigned to ", n_portfolio, " × ", n_portfolio, " portfolios based on asset growth rank (x-axis) and size rank (y-axis), both expressed as percentiles. Colors indicate portfolio cell assignment. The univariate sort (left) assigns portfolios on asset growth alone; the independent bivariate sort (center) assigns each dimension independently; the dependent bivariate sort (right) sorts on size first, then on asset growth within size groups."), fig.width=6.5, fig.height=3, fig.align="center", out.width="90%"}
common_theme <- list(
  scale_x_continuous(
    labels = scales::percent,
    breaks = breakpoints_ag,
    expand = c(0.01, 0)
  ),
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, expand = c(0.01, 0)),
  labs(x = "Asset growth rank", y = "Size rank"),
  theme(
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0),
    plot.title.position = "plot",
    plot.margin = margin(5.5, 14, 5.5, 5.5)
  )
)

p1 <- portfolios_univariate |>
  ggplot(aes(
    x = asset_growth,
    y = mktcap_lag,
    color = as.factor(ag_portfolio)
  )) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, size = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "Univariate sort") +
  common_theme

p2 <- portfolios_independent |>
  ggplot(aes(x = asset_growth, y = mktcap_lag, color = portfolio_cell)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, size = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "Independent\nbivariate sort") +
  common_theme

p3 <- portfolios_dependent |>
  ggplot(aes(x = asset_growth, y = mktcap_lag, color = portfolio_cell)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, size = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "Dependent\nbivariate sort") +
  common_theme

p1 +
  p2 +
  p3 +
  plot_layout(guides = "collect", axes = "collect_y")
```

`compute_long_short_returns()` takes the output of `compute_portfolio_returns()` and computes the spread between the top and bottom portfolios. A `direction` argument controls the sign and defaults to `"top_minus_bottom"`. The function returns one long-short series per return measure available in the input, so the equal-weighted, value-weighted, and capped value-weighted spreads are produced together. This long-short return is the factor-mimicking spread that the asset-pricing literature typically takes as the object of interest.

For users who want the full pipeline in a single call, `implement_portfolio_sort()` wraps the four functions above. It takes a panel of stock data, one or two sorting variables, a sorting method, and a configuration object, and returns the panel of portfolio returns. The case study below pipes this panel to `compute_long_short_returns()` to obtain the long-short factor series. The lower-level functions remain available for custom workflows that need finer control over breakpoints, weighting, or rebalancing.

# A case study in factor construction {#sec:ag}

We walk through the construction of the asset growth factor from raw CRSP and Compustat data to long-short portfolio returns, applying each stage of Table \@ref(tab:functions) in turn.

Load \CRANpkg{tidyfinance} together with a minimal set of supporting packages: \CRANpkg{dplyr} [@dplyr] for data manipulation, \CRANpkg{tidyr} [@tidyr] for reshaping between long and wide formats, and \CRANpkg{lubridate} [@lubridate] for date arithmetic.

```{r load-package, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, cache=FALSE}
library("tidyfinance")
library("dplyr")
library("tidyr")
library("lubridate")
```

## Data acquisition {#sec:data-download}

Constructing the asset growth factor requires two WRDS panels: annual accounting data from Compustat to compute the asset growth signal and monthly stock returns from CRSP to translate the signal into portfolio returns.

CRSP and Compustat are proprietary and require a WRDS subscription. All numbers, tables, and figures in this paper are computed from the real WRDS data with `data_domain <- "WRDS"`. 

```{r set-data-domain}
data_domain <- "WRDS"
```

Readers without a WRDS subscription can render the entire manuscript by setting `data_domain <- "Pseudo Data"` in the chunk above. Every `download_data()` call for the three WRDS datasets of the case study (monthly CRSP returns, annual Compustat fundamentals, and the CRSP-Compustat links) then returns simulated data from an in-package generator. The pseudo data keep the column names, data types, missingness patterns, and panel structure of the real data, so the cleaning, lagging, and sorting code runs through the same branches and every table and figure renders. They do not keep economic relations: returns are independent draws, so the long-short premia are noise. The `seed` argument makes the draws reproducible, and `n_assets` sets the size of the cross-section (default `1000L`).

```{r set-date-range}
date_start <- as.Date("1972-01-01")
date_end <- as.Date("2024-12-31")
```

We restrict the sample to the period from `r year(date_start)` onward, before which Compustat's coverage of the cross-section is sparser, and we end it in December `r year(date_end)`.

First, we download monthly stock returns from CRSP. Setting `add_ccm_links = TRUE` appends CRSP-Compustat linking identifiers needed to merge with financial statement data in the next step.

```{r download-crsp}
crsp_monthly <- download_data(
  domain = data_domain,
  dataset = "crsp_monthly",
  version = "v2",
  start_date = date_start,
  end_date = date_end,
  add_ccm_links = TRUE,
  quiet = TRUE
)
```

The dataset contains `r format(nrow(crsp_monthly), big.mark = ",")` stock-month observations for `r format(length(unique(crsp_monthly$permno)), big.mark = ",")` unique stocks, covering the period from `r format_pretty_date(min(crsp_monthly$date))` to `r format_pretty_date(max(crsp_monthly$calculation_date))`.

Next, we download annual financial statements from Compustat.

```{r download-compustat}
compustat_annual <- download_data(
  domain = data_domain,
  dataset = "compustat_annual",
  start_date = date_start,
  end_date = date_end,
  additional_columns = c("at", "ib"),
  only_usd = TRUE,
  quiet = TRUE
) |>
  select(gvkey, date, at, ib)
```

Annual Compustat data contain `r format(nrow(compustat_annual), big.mark = ",")` firm-year observations for `r format(length(unique(compustat_annual$gvkey)), big.mark = ",")` unique firms, covering the period from `r format_pretty_date(date_start)` to `r format_pretty_date(date_end)`. The `additional_columns` argument retrieves total assets (`at`) and income before extraordinary items (`ib`), needed for computing asset growth and applying an earnings filter in later steps. Setting `only_usd = TRUE` restricts the dataset to USD-denominated stocks.

## Variable construction {#sec:data-cleaning}

We illustrate data cleaning and variable construction using asset growth (AG) as our running example. Asset growth for a firm $i$ in year $t$ is the year-over-year percentage change in total assets [@cooper.2008],

$$
AG_{t,i} = (AT_{t,i} - AT_{t-1,i}) / AT_{t-1,i}\text{,}
$$

where $AT_{t,i}$ is total assets for firm $i$ in year $t$ (retrieved in column `at`).

The `add_lagged_columns()` function from \CRANpkg{tidyfinance} handles temporal alignment by creating a lagged version of total assets grouped by firm identifier (`gvkey`) with a one-year lag. Non-finite values (arising when lagged total assets are zero or missing) become `NA`.

```{r compute-sorting-variables}
sorting_variable_data <- compustat_annual |>
  add_lagged_columns(
    cols = "at",
    lag = years(1),
    by = "gvkey"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    asset_growth = (at - at_lag) / at_lag,
    asset_growth = if_else(is.finite(asset_growth), asset_growth, NA_real_)
  ) |>
  select(gvkey, date, asset_growth, ib)
```

The call relies on two silent defaults: `max_lag` falls back to `lag` (here one year), so only the single observation exactly one year before each row is eligible; `ff_adjustment = FALSE`, so the look-back is the plain calendar window.

`sorting_variable_data` contains one observation per firm-year, the natural unit for cross-sectional analysis of annual accounting variables. Asset growth is heavily right-skewed: a small number of firms with dramatic balance-sheet expansions generate extreme positive values. Table \@ref(tab:ag-summary) reports the pooled cross-sectional summary alongside the time-series average, minimum, and maximum of the corresponding statistic computed cross-sectionally each year.^[The pooled count of `r format(sum(!is.na(sorting_variable_data$asset_growth)), big.mark = ",")` firm-years is below the `r format(nrow(compustat_annual), big.mark = ",")` downloaded in Section \@ref(sec:data-download) because asset growth needs total assets in both the current fiscal year and the one exactly twelve months earlier; firm-years with missing total assets, each firm's first year, and gaps or changes in fiscal year-end all drop out.] We obtain both views with `create_summary_statistics()`, a \CRANpkg{tidyfinance} helper that returns the standard set of cross-sectional summary statistics for a variable: applied to the pooled (winsorized) sample for the first column and grouped by calendar year for the next three. Table \@ref(tab:ag-summary) assembles the two computations side by side.

```{r ag-summary-prep}
pooled_stats <- sorting_variable_data |>
  drop_na(asset_growth) |>
  mutate(asset_growth = winsorize(asset_growth, 0.01)) |>
  create_summary_statistics(asset_growth, detail = TRUE)

yearly_stats <- sorting_variable_data |>
  drop_na(asset_growth) |>
  group_by(year = year(date)) |>
  mutate(asset_growth = winsorize(asset_growth, 0.01)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  create_summary_statistics(asset_growth, by = year, detail = TRUE)
```

```{r ag-summary, echo=FALSE}
stat_cols <- c("n", "mean", "sd", "q10", "q25", "q50", "q75", "q90")
stat_labels <- c("N", "Mean", "SD", "P10", "P25", "Median", "P75", "P90")
fmt_val <- function(col, x) {
  if (col == "n") {
    formatC(round(x), format = "d", big.mark = ",")
  } else {
    formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 3)
  }
}

data.frame(
  Statistic = stat_labels,
  Pooled = vapply(
    stat_cols,
    function(s) fmt_val(s, pooled_stats[[s]]),
    character(1)
  ),
  `Yearly Mean` = vapply(
    stat_cols,
    function(s) fmt_val(s, mean(yearly_stats[[s]])),
    character(1)
  ),
  `Yearly Min` = vapply(
    stat_cols,
    function(s) fmt_val(s, min(yearly_stats[[s]])),
    character(1)
  ),
  `Yearly Max` = vapply(
    stat_cols,
    function(s) fmt_val(s, max(yearly_stats[[s]])),
    character(1)
  ),
  row.names = NULL,
  check.names = FALSE
) |>
  knitr::kable(
    caption = paste0(
      "Cross-sectional summary statistics for asset growth (winsorized at the 1st and 99th percentiles). The 'Pooled' column reports the statistic computed on the entire firm-year sample. The 'Yearly' columns summarize the time series of statistic values computed cross-sectionally year by year, taking the mean, minimum, and maximum across calendar years. N is the count of firm-year observations (pooled) or per-year observations (yearly columns). Sample: ",
      sample_years(drop_na(sorting_variable_data, asset_growth)),
      "."
    ),
    align = "lrrrr",
    format = "latex",
    booktabs = TRUE,
    linesep = ""
  )
```

The next step uses `join_lagged_values()` to merge the annual sorting variables onto the monthly CRSP panel. Setting `ff_adjustment = TRUE` implements the Fama-French convention [@fama.1993]: the accounting data of a fiscal year ending in calendar year $t$ are used from July of $t+1$ through June of $t+2$, whatever the month of the fiscal year-end. Every firm therefore updates in July, and no lag window is needed.

```{r lag-sorting-variables}
sorting_data <- crsp_monthly |>
  join_lagged_values(
    new_data = sorting_variable_data,
    id_keys = "gvkey",
    ff_adjustment = TRUE
  ) |>
  select(
    date,
    permno,
    exchange,
    siccd,
    ret_excess,
    mktcap_lag,
    asset_growth,
    ib
  ) |>
  filter(date >= date_start + months(12) + months(18))
```

The filter drops the first year, which only serves to compute growth rates, and the following 18 months, in which the lagged signal is not yet available. The columns `siccd` and `ib` support the sample filters in Section \@ref(sec:customized-sorts).

Figure \@ref(fig:ag-percentiles) shows the 33rd, 50th, and 66th cross-sectional percentiles of asset growth over time in the resulting panel; both the median and the dispersion across firms vary substantially over the sample.

```{r ag-percentiles, fig.alt="Time-series line plot of the 33rd, 50th, and 66th percentiles of cross-sectional asset growth, expressed as annual percentage growth in total assets.", fig.cap=paste0("Selected percentiles (33rd, 50th, 66th) of cross-sectional asset growth over time. The y-axis reports annual growth in total assets in percent. Sample: ", sample_years(drop_na(sorting_data)), "."), fig.width=6.5, fig.height=3, out.width="100%", echo=FALSE}
plot_data <- sorting_data |>
  drop_na() |>
  group_by(date) |>
  summarize(
    "33%" = quantile(asset_growth, 0.33),
    "Median" = quantile(asset_growth, 0.50),
    "66%" = quantile(asset_growth, 0.66),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -date,
    names_to = "quantile",
    values_to = "asset_growth"
  )

label_data <- plot_data |>
  group_by(quantile) |>
  slice_max(date, n = 1) |>
  mutate(date = date %m+% months(6)) |>
  ungroup()

ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = date, y = asset_growth, color = quantile)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_text(
    data = label_data,
    aes(label = quantile),
    hjust = 0,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_x_date(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.12))) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Asset growth") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

With the sorting variable constructed and merged onto the monthly stock panel, we now turn to portfolio sorts, the mechanism that translates firm-level characteristics into tradable factor returns.

## Portfolio sorting {#sec:portfolio-sorts}

In portfolio sorts, stocks are ranked each period by their sorting variable and divided into portfolios. Portfolio returns are equal-weighted or value-weighted averages of constituent stock returns. The long-short factor return is the difference between the extreme portfolios. For asset growth, the relevant spread is bottom minus top, reflecting the negative premium documented by @cooper.2008. The construction involves several methodological choices: which stocks enter the universe, how many portfolios to form, which exchange determines the breakpoints, the weighting scheme, and the rebalancing frequency.

`implement_portfolio_sort()` exposes all of these choices through a single function call. The function takes the panel data, one or two sorting variables, a sorting method, and a `portfolio_sort_options` object that bundles two configuration layers: `filter_options()` controls which observations enter the breakpoint and return computation (for example, excluding financial firms or stocks below a minimum price), and `breakpoint_options()` controls how portfolios are formed (number of portfolios, exchange universe, bunching). Internally, the function applies the sample filters and then calls `compute_portfolio_returns()`, which produces the time series of portfolio returns. A subsequent call to `compute_long_short_returns()` constructs the long-short portfolio.

`compute_portfolio_returns()` itself rests on two lower-level helpers, `compute_breakpoints()` for quantile cutoffs and `assign_portfolio()` for mapping each stock-month to a portfolio number. Both are exported, so researchers who need finer control can call them directly rather than through the wrapper. The two examples below use `implement_portfolio_sort()` throughout.

### Baseline specification (univariate sorts) {#sec:baseline-sorts}

The simplest call to `implement_portfolio_sort()` requires only a `portfolio_sort_options` object that specifies how to form the breakpoints. In a univariate sort, stocks are ranked on a single characteristic. We illustrate using asset growth as the sorting variable, forming quintile portfolios with breakpoints computed from NYSE-listed stocks only, and rebalancing annually in July.

```{r baseline-options}
options_baseline <- portfolio_sort_options(
  breakpoint_options_main = breakpoint_options(
    n_portfolios = 5,
    breakpoints_exchanges = "NYSE"
  )
)
```

```{r baseline-sort}
portfolio_returns <- implement_portfolio_sort(
  data = sorting_data,
  sorting_variables = "asset_growth",
  sorting_method = "univariate",
  rebalancing_month = 7,
  portfolio_sort_options = options_baseline
)
```

Apart from setting five portfolios, NYSE breakpoints, and `rebalancing_month = 7`, every other choice point falls back to the package default: a cap-weight cutoff at the 80th percentile of NYSE market capitalization for the capped value-weighted return, no minimum portfolio size, and no smooth bunching. Setting `rebalancing_month = 7` reforms the portfolios each July and holds them for twelve months, the month in which `ff_adjustment = TRUE` makes a new fiscal-year value available.

`implement_portfolio_sort()` returns one row per portfolio-month with the value-weighted (VW), equal-weighted (EW), and capped value-weighted (VWC) returns. With `direction = "bottom_minus_top"`, `compute_long_short_returns()` turns them into the factor, long low-AG and short high-AG stocks.

```{r long-short-ag}
factor_returns_ag <- portfolio_returns |>
  compute_long_short_returns(direction = "bottom_minus_top")
```

Table \@ref(tab:univariate-sort-ag) summarizes the time series of each quintile across all three weighting schemes, with the long-short portfolio appended as the final row.

```{r univariate-sort-ag-stats}
return_summary <- function(data) {
  data |>
    drop_na() |>
    summarize(
      across(
        c(ret_excess_vw, ret_excess_ew, ret_excess_vw_capped),
        list(
          mean = \(x) mean(x) * 12,
          tstat = \(x) mean(x) / (sd(x) / sqrt(n()))
        ),
        .names = "{.col}_{.fn}"
      ),
      .groups = "drop"
    )
}
univariate_sort_table <- bind_rows(
  portfolio_returns |>
    group_by(portfolio) |>
    return_summary() |>
    mutate(portfolio = as.character(portfolio)),
  factor_returns_ag |>
    return_summary() |>
    mutate(portfolio = "L/S")
)
```

```{r univariate-sort-ag, echo=FALSE}
group_header <- paste0(
  " & \\multicolumn{2}{c}{Value-weighted} & ",
  "\\multicolumn{2}{c}{Equal-weighted} & ",
  "\\multicolumn{2}{c}{Capped value-weighted} \\\\\n",
  "\\cmidrule(lr){2-3} \\cmidrule(lr){4-5} \\cmidrule(lr){6-7}\n"
)

raw_table <- univariate_sort_table |>
  knitr::kable(
    caption = paste0(
      "Time-series averages of annualized monthly excess returns for asset growth quintile portfolios. Portfolios are formed annually in July using NYSE breakpoints. Means are annualized (multiplied by 12). The $t$~statistic tests whether the mean monthly excess return differs from zero. Capped value-weighted caps market capitalization at the 80th percentile of NYSE stocks. The L/S row is the long-short portfolio (bottom minus top quintile). Sample: ",
      sample_years(drop_na(portfolio_returns)),
      "."
    ),
    digits = 3,
    escape = FALSE,
    format = "latex",
    booktabs = TRUE,
    linesep = "",
    col.names = c(
      "Portfolio",
      "Mean",
      "$t$~statistic",
      "Mean",
      "$t$~statistic",
      "Mean",
      "$t$~statistic"
    )
  )

structure(
  sub(
    "\\toprule\n",
    paste0("\\toprule\n", group_header),
    raw_table,
    fixed = TRUE
  ),
  format = attr(raw_table, "format"),
  class = class(raw_table)
)
```

The value-weighted long-short portfolio earns `r round(mean(factor_returns_ag$ret_excess_vw, na.rm = TRUE) * 12 * 100, 1)`% per year ($t$-statistic of `r round(mean(factor_returns_ag$ret_excess_vw, na.rm = TRUE) / (sd(factor_returns_ag$ret_excess_vw, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(sum(!is.na(factor_returns_ag$ret_excess_vw)))), 2)`). The sign matches @cooper.2008, which we discuss more below. The equal-weighted spread is considerably larger, which indicates that the effect is stronger among the small stocks that equal weighting emphasizes. Mean returns decline from the lowest to the highest AG quintile under all three weighting schemes, monotonically for equal and capped value weights and with nearly equal third and fourth quintiles for value weights. A single function call thus recovers the negative relation between asset growth and subsequent returns from raw WRDS data.

### Customized specification (bivariate sorts) {#sec:customized-sorts}

The baseline specification above takes nearly every package default and runs a univariate sort to form long-short portfolios. The customized specification below changes both: it overrides several of those defaults through `portfolio_sort_options` and moves from sorting on one variable to sorting on two.

We adopt a specification that combines, in a single call to `implement_portfolio_sort()`, the universe restrictions and breakpoint conventions used in many empirical studies: exclude financials and utilities, exclude firms with non-positive earnings, ignore the smallest 20% of NYSE-listed firms when computing breakpoints, form quintiles on AG within size buckets, use NYSE-only breakpoints, rebalance annually in July, and require at least ten constituents per portfolio.

Bivariate sorts control for a second variable, typically firm size (`mktcap_lag`), when forming portfolios on the main characteristic. We use the dependent variant introduced in Section \@ref(sec:portfolio-sorting): stocks are first split into size buckets, then sorted into asset growth portfolios within each bucket, with returns averaged across the size dimension.

```{r customized-options}
options_customized <- portfolio_sort_options(
  filter_options = filter_options(
    exclude_financials = TRUE,
    exclude_utilities = TRUE,
    exclude_negative_earnings = TRUE
  ),
  breakpoint_options_main = breakpoint_options(
    n_portfolios = 5,
    breakpoints_exchanges = "NYSE",
    breakpoints_min_size_threshold = 0.2
  ),
  breakpoint_options_secondary = breakpoint_options(
    n_portfolios = 2,
    breakpoints_exchanges = "NYSE"
  )
)
```

```{r customized-sort}
portfolio_returns_customized <- implement_portfolio_sort(
  data = sorting_data,
  sorting_variables = c("asset_growth", "mktcap_lag"),
  sorting_method = "bivariate-dependent",
  rebalancing_month = 7,
  portfolio_sort_options = options_customized,
  min_portfolio_size = 10,
  quiet = TRUE
)
factor_returns_customized <- portfolio_returns_customized |>
  compute_long_short_returns(direction = "bottom_minus_top")
```

A single options object (`options_customized`) bundles every methodological choice that distinguishes this specification from the baseline; nothing in the surrounding pipeline changes. Setting `quiet = TRUE` suppresses the messages that report how many observations each filter drops. With annual rebalancing, the screens apply in the formation month only, so a stock that, for example, reports a loss after formation keeps its returns until the portfolios are reformed. `filter_options(timing = "every_period")` applies the screens in every month instead, but this uses information that is not available at formation and the package warns about it.

For comparison, we also include a bivariate-dependent sort that uses the default filters and breakpoint conventions, so the only difference from the baseline is the addition of size control. The long-short returns from that specification are appended to the customized one in Table \@ref(tab:customized-comparison).

```{r bivariate-only-sort}
options_bivariate <- portfolio_sort_options(
  breakpoint_options_main = breakpoint_options(
    n_portfolios = 5,
    breakpoints_exchanges = "NYSE"
  ),
  breakpoint_options_secondary = breakpoint_options(
    n_portfolios = 2,
    breakpoints_exchanges = "NYSE"
  )
)
portfolio_returns_bivariate <- implement_portfolio_sort(
  data = sorting_data,
  sorting_variables = c("asset_growth", "mktcap_lag"),
  sorting_method = "bivariate-dependent",
  rebalancing_month = 7,
  portfolio_sort_options = options_bivariate
)
factor_returns_bivariate <- portfolio_returns_bivariate |>
  compute_long_short_returns(direction = "bottom_minus_top")
```

Table \@ref(tab:customized-comparison) also reports two sensitivity checks of the baseline, each a one-argument change. The first drops `ff_adjustment` and uses a plain lag window instead: each month receives the most recent fiscal-year value observed 7 to 18 months earlier, so each firm updates seven months after its own fiscal year-end rather than in July. The second caps market capitalization at the 80th percentile of all stocks instead of NYSE stocks, which only affects the capped value-weighted returns.

```{r sensitivity-sorts}
sorting_data_window <- crsp_monthly |>
  join_lagged_values(
    new_data = sorting_variable_data,
    id_keys = "gvkey",
    min_lag = months(7),
    max_lag = months(18)
  ) |>
  filter(date >= date_start + months(12) + months(18))

factor_returns_window <- implement_portfolio_sort(
  data = sorting_data_window,
  sorting_variables = "asset_growth",
  sorting_method = "univariate",
  rebalancing_month = 7,
  portfolio_sort_options = options_baseline
) |>
  compute_long_short_returns(direction = "bottom_minus_top")

factor_returns_all_cap <- implement_portfolio_sort(
  data = sorting_data,
  sorting_variables = "asset_growth",
  sorting_method = "univariate",
  rebalancing_month = 7,
  portfolio_sort_options = options_baseline,
  cap_weight_exchanges = NULL
) |>
  compute_long_short_returns(direction = "bottom_minus_top")
```

```{r customized-comparison-stats, echo=FALSE}
summarize_spread <- function(data, specification) {
  data |>
    drop_na() |>
    summarize(
      Specification = specification,
      `VW mean` = mean(ret_excess_vw) * 12,
      `VW $t$` = mean(ret_excess_vw) / (sd(ret_excess_vw) / sqrt(n())),
      `VWC mean` = mean(ret_excess_vw_capped) * 12,
      `VWC $t$` = mean(ret_excess_vw_capped) /
        (sd(ret_excess_vw_capped) / sqrt(n()))
    )
}
customized_comparison_table <- bind_rows(
  summarize_spread(factor_returns_ag, "Baseline (univariate, no filters)"),
  summarize_spread(
    factor_returns_bivariate,
    "Bivariate only (size-controlled, no filters)"
  ),
  summarize_spread(
    factor_returns_customized,
    "Customized (size-controlled, filtered)"
  ),
  summarize_spread(factor_returns_window, "Baseline, 7-to-18-month window"),
  summarize_spread(factor_returns_all_cap, "Baseline, all-stock cap")
)
```

Table \@ref(tab:customized-comparison) decomposes the customized premium into two layers. Adding the size-controlled bivariate sort alone (the bivariate-only row) barely moves the annualized premium, from `r sprintf("%.1f", customized_comparison_table[[2]][1] * 100)`% to `r sprintf("%.1f", customized_comparison_table[[2]][2] * 100)`%, but raises the $t$-statistic from `r sprintf("%.2f", customized_comparison_table[[3]][1])` to `r sprintf("%.2f", customized_comparison_table[[3]][2])`, because the size-controlled spread is less volatile. Layering the filter set and the 20% breakpoint threshold on top lowers the premium to `r sprintf("%.1f", customized_comparison_table[[2]][3] * 100)`% with a $t$-statistic of `r sprintf("%.2f", customized_comparison_table[[3]][3])`, which is no longer significant at the 5% level: removing financials, utilities, and loss-making firms and computing breakpoints without the smallest 20% of NYSE firms weakens the spread. In the sensitivity checks, the plain lag window gives a value-weighted premium of `r sprintf("%.1f", customized_comparison_table[[2]][4] * 100)`% ($t$-statistic of `r sprintf("%.2f", customized_comparison_table[[3]][4])`) instead of `r sprintf("%.1f", customized_comparison_table[[2]][1] * 100)`%, and capping at the all-stock percentile changes the capped value-weighted premium from `r sprintf("%.1f", customized_comparison_table[[4]][1] * 100)`% ($t$-statistic of `r sprintf("%.2f", customized_comparison_table[[5]][1])`) to `r sprintf("%.1f", customized_comparison_table[[4]][5] * 100)`% ($t$-statistic of `r sprintf("%.2f", customized_comparison_table[[5]][5])`). Across the three main specifications, the spread has the sign of the negative AG premium in @cooper.2008, but is considerably smaller than their annual value-weighted long-short premium of about 12.6% over July 1968 to June 2003, which is based on deciles rather than quintiles.[^cooper-deciles]

[^cooper-deciles]: @cooper.2008 sorts into deciles.


```{r customized-comparison, echo=FALSE}
customized_comparison_table |>
  knitr::kable(
    caption = paste0(
      "Comparison of long-short asset growth returns across three specifications and two sensitivity checks of the baseline. The baseline is a univariate sort with NYSE breakpoints and no filters. The bivariate-only specification adds a dependent bivariate sort on size to the baseline but otherwise keeps the same universe and breakpoints. The customized specification adds the filter set (financials, utilities, non-positive earnings) and a 20\\% size threshold on the breakpoints. The last two rows change one choice of the baseline: a 7-to-18-month lag window instead of the Fama-French timing, and a cap at the 80th percentile of all stocks instead of NYSE stocks. All rows use annual July rebalancing; means are annualized value-weighted (VW) and capped value-weighted (VWC) excess returns. Sample: ",
      sample_years(drop_na(factor_returns_ag)),
      "."
    ),
    digits = 3,
    escape = FALSE,
    format = "latex",
    booktabs = TRUE,
    linesep = ""
  )
```

The lower-level functions in Table \@ref(tab:functions) share their arguments with `implement_portfolio_sort()`, so researchers can unroll the wrapper when custom logic applies at one stage only, for example, breakpoints computed within each industry or from a trailing window.

### Staggered rebalancing {#sec:staggered}

Some factors are built with *staggered* rebalancing instead of a single annual or monthly formation date: portfolios are formed every month, and each cohort is held for $K$ months, so that $K$ overlapping cohorts are held at any time. @jegadeesh.1993 construct momentum this way. Their $J$/$K$ strategies sort stocks on the past $J$-month return and hold each cohort for $K$ months. In \CRANpkg{tidyfinance}, the `holding_period` argument sets $K$. We compute the six-month momentum signal on calendar months with `compute_rolling_value()`, which requires all six months to be observed, and lag it by one month, so that the signal of month $t$ uses returns up to month $t-1$ only.

```{r momentum-signal}
momentum_data <- crsp_monthly |>
  arrange(permno, date) |>
  group_by(permno) |>
  mutate(
    momentum = compute_rolling_value(
      pick(date, ret),
      \(x) prod(1 + x$ret) - 1,
      periods = 6
    )
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  add_lagged_columns(cols = "momentum", lag = months(1), by = "permno")
```

We then form decile portfolios on NYSE breakpoints and vary the holding period over $K \in \{1, 3, 6, 12\}$ months, where $K = 1$ is plain monthly rebalancing.

```{r momentum-sorts}
options_momentum <- portfolio_sort_options(
  breakpoint_options_main = breakpoint_options(
    n_portfolios = 10,
    breakpoints_exchanges = "NYSE"
  )
)
momentum_returns <- tibble(holding_period = c(1, 3, 6, 12)) |>
  mutate(
    factor_returns = purrr::map(
      holding_period,
      \(k) {
        implement_portfolio_sort(
          data = momentum_data,
          sorting_variables = "momentum_lag",
          sorting_method = "univariate",
          holding_period = k,
          portfolio_sort_options = options_momentum,
          quiet = TRUE
        ) |>
          compute_long_short_returns(direction = "top_minus_bottom")
      }
    )
  )
```

```{r momentum-stats, echo=FALSE}
momentum_table <- momentum_returns |>
  mutate(
    stats = purrr::map(
      factor_returns,
      \(x) {
        x |>
          drop_na(ret_excess_ew, ret_excess_vw) |>
          summarize(
            `EW mean` = mean(ret_excess_ew) * 12,
            `EW $t$` = mean(ret_excess_ew) / (sd(ret_excess_ew) / sqrt(n())),
            `VW mean` = mean(ret_excess_vw) * 12,
            `VW $t$` = mean(ret_excess_vw) / (sd(ret_excess_vw) / sqrt(n()))
          )
      }
    )
  ) |>
  select(`Holding period $K$` = holding_period, stats) |>
  unnest(stats)
```

```{r momentum, echo=FALSE}
momentum_table |>
  knitr::kable(
    caption = paste0(
      "Long-short momentum returns with staggered rebalancing. Stocks are sorted into deciles on their lagged six-month return ($J = 6$) using NYSE breakpoints, and each monthly cohort is held for $K$ months; $K = 1$ is monthly rebalancing. The long-short portfolio buys the top decile (winners) and sells the bottom decile (losers). Means are annualized equal-weighted (EW) and value-weighted (VW) excess returns. Sample: ",
      sample_years(drop_na(momentum_returns$factor_returns[[1]])),
      "."
    ),
    digits = 3,
    escape = FALSE,
    format = "latex",
    booktabs = TRUE,
    linesep = ""
  )
```

Table \@ref(tab:momentum) shows that the holding period matters. With monthly rebalancing ($K = 1$), the equal-weighted momentum spread is `r sprintf("%.1f", momentum_table[["EW mean"]][1] * 100)`% per year ($t$-statistic of `r sprintf("%.2f", momentum_table[["EW $t$"]][1])`). Holding six overlapping cohorts, as in @jegadeesh.1993, raises it to `r sprintf("%.1f", momentum_table[["EW mean"]][3] * 100)`% ($t$-statistic of `r sprintf("%.2f", momentum_table[["EW $t$"]][3])`), and the value-weighted spread to `r sprintf("%.1f", momentum_table[["VW mean"]][3] * 100)`% ($t$-statistic of `r sprintf("%.2f", momentum_table[["VW $t$"]][3])`). The signal, the breakpoints, and the rest of the call are identical across rows; only `holding_period` changes.

### Asset pricing tests {#sec:fama-macbeth}
 
A long-short return is one summary of whether asset growth predicts the cross-section of returns. A complementary view comes from Fama-MacBeth regressions [@fama.1973], which estimate the average risk premium associated with a characteristic after running cross-sectional regressions period by period. \CRANpkg{tidyfinance} implements the standard procedure in `estimate_fama_macbeth()`, which takes a panel and a model formula, fits one cross-sectional ordinary least squares (OLS) regression per period, and aggregates the period-level coefficients into average risk premia with @newey.1987 standard errors. By default, these are the standard errors of `NeweyWest()` from \CRANpkg{sandwich} [@zeileis.2004]: the time series of coefficients is prewhitened with a first-order vector autoregression, and the bandwidth is selected automatically following @newey.1994.

Here, we winsorize the AG signal at the 1st and 99th percentiles to keep extreme observations from dominating the cross-sectional regressions and pair it with log market capitalization as a size control and the lagged six-month momentum signal of Section \@ref(sec:staggered).
 
```{r fama-macbeth-data}
fm_data <- sorting_data |>
  left_join(
    momentum_data |>
      select(permno, date, momentum_lag),
    join_by(permno, date)
  ) |>
  drop_na(asset_growth, mktcap_lag, momentum_lag, ret_excess) |>
  group_by(date) |>
  mutate(
    asset_growth = winsorize(x = asset_growth, cut = 0.01),
    log_mktcap = log(mktcap_lag)
  ) |>
  ungroup()
```
 
```{r fama-macbeth-fit}
fm_results <- estimate_fama_macbeth(
  data = fm_data,
  model = "ret_excess ~ asset_growth + log_mktcap + momentum_lag"
)
```
 
```{r fama-macbeth, echo=FALSE}
fm_results |>
  mutate(
    factor = recode(
      factor,
      "intercept" = "Intercept",
      "asset_growth" = "Asset growth",
      "log_mktcap" = "Log market cap",
      "momentum_lag" = "Momentum"
    )
  ) |>
  select(
    Variable = factor,
    `Risk premium` = risk_premium,
    SE = standard_error,
    `$t$~statistic` = t_statistic,
    `N (months)` = n
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(
    caption = paste0(
      "Fama-MacBeth regression of monthly excess returns on lagged asset growth, lagged log market capitalization, and lagged six-month momentum. Coefficients are time-series averages of monthly cross-sectional OLS estimates; standard errors are Newey and West (1987) with first-order vector autoregressive prewhitening and the automatic bandwidth of Newey and West (1994). The intercept and slopes on the right-hand-side variables are reported on the monthly scale. Sample: ",
      sample_years(fm_data),
      "."
    ),
    digits = 4,
    escape = FALSE,
    format = "latex",
    booktabs = TRUE,
    linesep = ""
  )
```

The negative slope on `asset_growth` in Table \@ref(tab:fama-macbeth) lines up with the long-short evidence in Table \@ref(tab:univariate-sort-ag) and Table \@ref(tab:customized-comparison): high-AG firms earn lower subsequent returns, conditional on size and momentum. As an external benchmark, @cooper.2008 [Table III, Panel A, Model 1] reports a Fama-MacBeth slope on annual asset growth of -0.0922 ($t$-statistic of -6.52). Dividing by 12 gives a rough monthly counterpart of `r round(-0.0922 / 12, 4)` $(=-0.0922/12)$. The comparison is only indicative, because @cooper.2008 regress annual returns and include additional controls.[^cooper-fm-controls] Switching to `vcov = "iid"` or supplying `vcov_options = list(lag = 6, prewhite = FALSE)` would change the standard-error treatment without altering the rest of the call, and adding additional regressors (e.g., a beta estimate from `estimate_betas()`, a profitability measure, an idiosyncratic-volatility control) is a one-line extension to the model formula. The same function therefore covers the standard cross-sectional asset-pricing test that complements the portfolio-sort evidence used throughout the rest of the paper.

[^cooper-fm-controls]: @cooper.2008 additionally control for book-to-market and 36-month past returns.

# Summary and discussion {#sec:summary}

Empirical asset pricing depends on dozens of construction choices that no consensus pins down. \CRANpkg{tidyfinance} makes those choices first-class objects in the workflow: each is an argument, each has a documented default, each can be varied without rebuilding the pipeline. Disagreements over construction become empirical questions, not implicit assumptions buried in code.

We maintain and extend the package on CRAN. Unit tests cover all functions, with 100% code coverage reported by [Codecov](https://app.codecov.io/gh/tidy-finance/r-tidyfinance), and each release passes R CMD check on the latest macOS, Windows, and Ubuntu. A scheduled GitHub Actions workflow refreshes the companion risk-free rate on Hugging Face.

Companion materials at [tidy-finance.org](https://tidy-finance.org) use \CRANpkg{tidyfinance} in open coursework for undergraduate and graduate finance and asset pricing in \proglang{R}. The site also hosts a reviewed channel through which researchers can publish replications and new construction routines, so the catalog of factors and conventions can grow with the literature.

We obtained the results in this paper using \proglang{R} `r r_version` with the following packages: \CRANpkg{tidyfinance} `r pkg_version("tidyfinance")`, \CRANpkg{dplyr} `r pkg_version("dplyr")` [@dplyr], \CRANpkg{tidyr} `r pkg_version("tidyr")` [@tidyr], \CRANpkg{ggplot2} `r pkg_version("ggplot2")` [@ggplot2], and \CRANpkg{lubridate} `r pkg_version("lubridate")` [@lubridate]. We install development versions of \CRANpkg{tidyfinance} with \CRANpkg{remotes} `r pkg_version("remotes")` [@remotes]. Figures additionally use \CRANpkg{scales} `r pkg_version("scales")` [@scales] and \CRANpkg{patchwork} `r pkg_version("patchwork")` [@patchwork]. CRAN hosts \proglang{R} and all packages at [https://CRAN.R-project.org/](https://CRAN.R-project.org/). \CRANpkg{renv} `r pkg_version("renv")` [@renv] ensures full reproducibility of the computational environment. Reproducing the factor return data requires an institutional subscription to WRDS, as the underlying CRSP and Compustat data are proprietary and cannot be redistributed.

Calling `rmarkdown::render("tidyfinance.Rmd")` renders the manuscript with WRDS data or pseudo data (Section \@ref(sec:data-download)). In the last render, running its code took `r render_minutes <- ceiling(as.numeric(difftime(Sys.time(), render_start, units = "mins"))); paste(render_minutes, if (render_minutes == 1) "minute" else "minutes")` or less. Timings reported here are obtained on `r sessionInfo()$running` with a `r parallel::detectCores()`-core processor running \proglang{R} `r r_version`; WRDS extracts are not pre-cached, so this figure includes the time to download the underlying CRSP and Compustat panels.
